uncited: Computes the center and radius of the unique circle passing through the three vertices of a triangle.

It serves as the geometric basis for defining bounding spheres in triangle-based volume rendering primitives, specifically within the [TetSplat](https://ken.museth.org/Publications_files/Museth-Lombeyda_VIS04.pdf) framework.

It is distinguished from the [Unsigned Triangle Distance](3587-unsigned-triangle-distance.md) method by providing a global bounding volume for the triangle rather than a point-to-surface distance metric.
**Inputs:** Three vertices $a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}^3$.
**Outputs:** Circum-center $C$ and circum-radius $R$.
No persistent data structures are required.
**Check for Degeneracy:** Compute the cross product magnitude $|A(b, c)|$.
If this value is near zero, the vertices are co-linear.
*   *Handling:* If degenerate, the method is undefined or requires fallback logic not specified in the primary formula.
**Check for Obtuseness:** Determine if the triangle is obtuse.
This avoids numerical instability associated with large circum-radii for obtuse triangles.
**Compute Relative Center:** For non-degenerate, non-obtuse triangles, calculate the relative circum-center $m_{tri}$ using the analytic formula.
**Compute Absolute Center:** $C = a + m_{tri}$.
*   $| \cdot |$ denotes the Euclidean norm.
Computes the center and radius of the sphere passing through four vertices $a, b, c, d$.
It uses a determinant-based formula involving cross products of edge vectors.
It is chosen when tetrahedral primitives are used instead of triangles.
*   **Time Complexity:** $O(1)$ constant time operations (vector arithmetic).
*   **Memory Complexity:** $O(1)$ auxiliary space.
*   **When to use:** When defining bounding spheres for triangle-based splats in volume rendering.
*   **When not to use:** For degenerate triangles or when a tighter bounding volume is required for obtuse triangles (use the midpoint fallback instead).
Originated in the TetSplat paper by Museth and Lombeyda (2004) for real-time rendering and volume clipping of large meshes.
The method is cited from reference [19] in the original paper, which is not explicitly named in the provided text but is implied to be a standard geometric computation reference.
It is used in the context of deriving leaf nodes for hierarchical volume representations from triangle meshes.
